title: Air Pollution and Primary Myocardial Infarction: An Ecological Study in a Low-Risk European Region
content: Background/Objectives: Air pollution (AP) has been linked to an increased risk of ischemic heart disease (IHD). Numerous studies have analysed the impact of AP on myocardial infarction (MI), yielding conflicting results that could be attributed to the selection of cases and regional differences in pollution and cardiovascular risk. Methods: The relationship between the incidence of ST-segment-MI with demonstrated culprit plaque (CP-STEMI) and the exposure to several air pollutants in previous days was studied in municipalities of the metropolitan area of Madrid (Spain, 2013-2018) using linear quasi-Poisson regressions. The municipality’s daily pollution exposure was estimated as the average of all AP measurement stations weighted by the inverse of the distance to the centroid of the municipality. Results: 4,406 CP-STEMI cases were registered. NO2 surpassed the World Health Organisation recommended level more than 50% of the days. Particulate matter <2.5 microns (PM2.5) surpassed recommended level 16% of the days and SO2 and CO none. For the two-day lag exposure model, there was a significant increase in CP-STEMI in days with an increase to the 2nd tertile vs the 1st tertile of PM2.5 (aRR 1.10, 95%CI:1.00-1.20, p=0.043). The difference between the 1st and 3rd tertiles remained positive but not significant. A clear association of CP-STEMI and cold was found, but not for the rest of pollutants. Conclusions: This study suggests an increased risk of CP-STEMI independently associated with PM2.5 and confirms the effect of cold, in a region with low risk of IHD, temperate climate and reasonably controlled levels of environmental pollution.
